questions.stem: Under a 30% quota share reinsurance treaty, the insurer accepts a group life scheme with annual premium of ₦60m and sum assured of ₦6bn. Three death claims total ₦450m. The reinsurer is required to pay:

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

Under a quota share treaty, the reinsurer shares a fixed percentage of all premiums and all claims. At 30% quota share:
• Reinsurer's share of premium: 30% × ₦60m = ₦18m (received by reinsurer)
• Reinsurer's share of claims: 30% × ₦450m = ₦135m (paid by reinsurer)
The reinsurer pays ₦135m and the cedant retains 70% of the claims (₦315m net).
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) ₦18m is the reinsurer's share of premium income, not its claims liability.
(C) ₦315m is the cedant's 70% retention of the claims — the cedant's net liability, not the reinsurer's payment.
(D) ₦450m is the total gross claims liability before reinsurance — the reinsurer pays only its quota share proportion.

questions.stem: Yearly Renewable Term (YRT) reinsurance provides the cedant insurer with:

opts.x: A proportionate share of the reinsurer's entire premium income and reserve.
Annual mortality cover on the Net Amount at Risk only, with the reserve retained by the cedant.
A guarantee that the reinsurer will accept all risks ceded without individual review.
Coverage for aggregate claims exceeding a defined percentage of premium income in any year.

questions.answer: (B) Annual mortality cover on the Net Amount at Risk only, with the reserve retained by the cedant.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

YRT (Yearly Renewable Term) reinsurance is a non-proportional mortality cover: the cedant cedes only the pure mortality risk (the Net Amount at Risk — the excess of the sum assured over the policy reserve) to the reinsurer. The cedant retains the full policy reserve on its balance sheet and continues to collect the full gross premium. The reinsurer charges an annual risk premium based on the NAR and the applicable mortality rate. The YRT premium is renegotiated annually at renewal, hence 'yearly renewable.'
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) describes co-insurance (proportional reinsurance) — where a fixed share of premium and reserve is ceded to the reinsurer. This is the opposite of YRT, which cedes no reserve.
(C) No reinsurance treaty guarantees automatic acceptance of all ceded risks without review. Facultative reinsurance is individually assessed; treaty reinsurance accepts within agreed parameters but does not guarantee individual case acceptance.
(D) describes a stop-loss (aggregate excess of loss) cover — triggered when total claims exceed a defined ratio of premiums. This is distinct from YRT, which is per-risk mortality cover, not aggregate cover.

questions.stem: The minimum paid-up capital requirement for reinsurance companies under NIIRA 2025 is:

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

Section 15(1)(c) of NIIRA 2025 sets the minimum capital for reinsurance business at ₦35 billion, or the risk-based capital determined by the Commission if higher. This represents a large increase from the prior ₦10 billion minimum and is intended to transform the domestic reinsurance market into a credible first-line capacity provider capable of retaining a materially larger proportion of Nigerian insurance risk.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) ₦10 billion is the minimum for life insurance companies — not reinsurers.
(B) ₦18 billion is not a NIIRA 2025 threshold: the Act sets no composite capital figure, and composite licences are no longer issued to insurers (s.6).
(D) ₦100 billion is not a NIIRA 2025 capital threshold for any licence category.

questions.stem: The Net Amount at Risk (NAR) on a life insurance policy is best defined as:

opts.x: The total sum assured payable on death.
The difference between the sum assured and the policy reserve at a given policy duration.
The reinsurer's maximum liability under the treaty in any single year.
The amount the insurer retains after paying all claims and expenses.

questions.answer: (B) The difference between the sum assured and the policy reserve at a given policy duration.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The NAR is the portion of the death benefit that the insurer is at risk of paying from current assets (not from accumulated reserves). If a policy has a sum assured of ₦10m and a policy reserve of ₦2.5m, the NAR is ₦10m − ₦2.5m = ₦7.5m. On death, the insurer would pay ₦10m total: ₦2.5m from the policy reserve (already set aside) and ₦7.5m from current assets. The YRT reinsurance covers the NAR because that is the additional risk the insurer bears beyond its accumulated reserve.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) The sum assured is the total death benefit — the NAR is a subset of the sum assured (the portion above the reserve).
(C) The reinsurer's maximum treaty liability is determined by treaty capacity limits — related to NAR but not the same concept.
(D) The net retained amount after claims and expenses is an accounting concept, not the actuarial NAR definition.

questions.stem: A reinsurance treaty under which the cedant retains all risks below ₦50 million and cedes only the amount of individual policy sum assured above ₦50 million is:

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

A surplus treaty is a proportional reinsurance arrangement in which the cedant retains a defined amount per risk (the 'retention' — ₦50m in this case) and cedes only the surplus above the retention. The surplus is distributed across the reinsurer's lines of capacity. Unlike quota share (which cedes a fixed percentage regardless of size), the surplus treaty cedes different amounts from different risks — a ₦100m policy cedes ₦50m (100%); a ₦60m policy cedes ₦10m (17%).
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) A quota share treaty cedes a fixed percentage of every risk — e.g., 30% of all risks regardless of size. It does not have a retention threshold below which nothing is ceded.
(B) A stop loss (aggregate excess of loss) treaty is triggered when total claims in a period exceed a defined percentage of premium income. It is an aggregate cover, not a per-risk excess-of-retention arrangement.
(D) An excess of loss treaty in life insurance is typically a per-life XL cover — attaching at a defined net retained amount per individual life (not the same as the surplus mechanism, which is proportional above the retention).

questions.stem:
A Nigerian life insurer has the following reinsurance programme: a YRT surplus treaty with a retention limit of ₦60m and 8 lines of capacity (₦480m maximum cession); and a per-life excess of loss cover attaching at ₦200m per life (net of treaty) with a maximum of ₦300m. An individual life policy for ₦700m is applied for.
(a) Show how the ₦700m risk is distributed among the cedant, the YRT reinsurer, and the XL reinsurer.
(b) Calculate the cedant’s net retained position after all reinsurance.
(c) Explain the purpose of combining a YRT surplus treaty with a per-life XL cover in this way.
(d) If the individual dies and the full ₦700m benefit falls due, calculate the recovery the cedant receives from each reinsurance layer.

model.h: Part (a) — Risk Distribution

The ₦700m risk is distributed as follows:

Cedant retention: ₦60m (the first layer — the surplus treaty's retention limit)

YRT surplus treaty cession: The surplus treaty has 8 lines of capacity. Each 'line' equals the retention (₦60m). Total surplus capacity: 8 × ₦60m = ₦480m. The surplus above the ₦60m retention is ceded: ₦700m − ₦60m = ₦640m. However, the treaty capacity is only ₦480m. So the surplus cession is capped at ₦480m.

Net of treaty (before XL): Cedant's position after surplus cession: ₦700m − ₦60m (retention) − ₦480m (surplus ceded) = ₦160m. But we specified the XL attaches at ₦200m net — since the net is ₦160m which is below the XL attachment, the XL does not attach on this risk. The remaining ₦160m net must either be retained by the cedant or individually reinsured (facultative placement).

Note for candidates: This structure reveals a coverage gap — the sum assured (₦700m) exceeds the total programme capacity (₦60m retention + ₦480m surplus = ₦540m), leaving ₦160m uncovered by treaty. The per-life XL only attaches at ₦200m net of treaty — but the net after surplus is only ₦160m. This is precisely why large individual risks (₦700m) typically require facultative reinsurance placement in addition to treaty coverage.
Part (b) — Cedant's Net Retained Position

After all treaty protections:
• Cedant retains ₦60m under the surplus treaty retention.
• ₦480m is ceded to the surplus treaty reinsurer.
• ₦160m is not covered by treaty (the gap between programme capacity and the risk size) — unless separately placed facultatively.
• The XL does not attach (net position ₦160m < ₦200m XL attachment point).

Net retained if no facultative: ₦60m + ₦160m = ₦220m
Net retained if facultative is placed for the ₦160m gap: ₦60m
Part (c) — Purpose of Combining YRT Surplus with Per-Life XL

The two layers serve complementary functions:

The YRT surplus treaty: Provides routine capacity for individual life policies that exceed the cedant's retention but fall within the treaty capacity. It efficiently handles the majority of above-retention risks with a simple proportional mechanism — the reinsurer takes a defined share of each risk.

The per-life XL cover: Addresses 'jumbo' risks — individual lives with sum assureds so large that they would exceed the surplus treaty's capacity if the cedant were to write them. The XL attaches at ₦200m net of treaty — so it only operates on risks where the cedant's net position after the surplus cession is still ₦200m+ (very large policies). Without the XL, such risks would require individual facultative reinsurance (slower, more expensive). The XL provides a standing capacity for the occasional very large individual risk.

The combined programme therefore: handles routine above-retention risks via the surplus treaty; handles exceptional very large risks via the XL; and avoids the expense and delay of facultative reinsurance for all but the largest and most complex individual cases.
Part (d) — Recovery from Each Layer on a Full ₦700m Death Claim

On the insured life's death, the full ₦700m benefit is payable. Recovery from each layer:
• Cedant's gross payment to beneficiary: ₦700m
• Recovery from surplus treaty reinsurer: ₦480m (their share of the ceded risk)
• XL recovery: ₦0 (XL did not attach — net of treaty is ₦160m, below the ₦200m attachment)
• Cedant's net cost: ₦700m − ₦480m = ₦220m

If facultative reinsurance had been placed for the ₦160m gap:
• Facultative reinsurer pays: ₦160m
• Cedant's net cost: ₦700m − ₦480m − ₦160m = ₦60m (the retention only)
Part (a) — What is Ceded

Co-insurance (proportional): The cedant cedes a defined percentage (e.g., 40%) of the policy in its entirety — premium income, policy reserve, and death benefit liability. The reinsurer effectively co-owns the policy. The reinsurer pays the cedant a ceding commission to compensate for the acquisition and administration costs the cedant bears.

YRT: The cedant cedes only the Net Amount at Risk (NAR) — the mortality risk above the policy reserve — on an annual basis. No reserve is ceded. The cedant pays the reinsurer an annual risk premium based on the NAR × the treaty mortality rate. The YRT is renewed each year (hence 'yearly renewable') and the NAR and premium change annually as the reserve grows and the NAR reduces.
Part (b) — Balance Sheet and Cash Flow Implications

Co-insurance:
• Balance sheet: The cedant's gross policy reserve is replaced by a lower net reserve (after the reinsured portion). The reinsurance asset (the ceded reserve) appears on the cedant's balance sheet.
• Cash flow: The cedant receives a large upfront ceding commission when the treaty is established; ongoing premium flows split proportionally between cedant and reinsurer.

YRT:
• Balance sheet: The full gross policy reserve remains on the cedant's balance sheet — YRT cedes no reserve. The reinsurance asset is the value of future YRT recoveries (mortality protection only).
• Cash flow: The cedant pays annual YRT risk premiums to the reinsurer — a regular outflow. No ceding commission is typically involved. YRT creates a smaller, more consistent cash flow impact than co-insurance.
Part (c) — More Appropriate for Pure Term Assurance

YRT is more appropriate for pure term assurance.

Reason: A term assurance policy accumulates minimal or zero reserve — the policy's value consists almost entirely of NAR throughout the term. Co-insurance of a term policy would cede only the mortality risk (since there is no reserve to cede) — functionally similar to YRT but less efficiently structured for a product without savings elements. YRT directly addresses the risk profile of term assurance: the NAR starts at or near the full sum assured and decreases slowly only in the very late years of the term. YRT pricing scales exactly with this NAR profile.
Part (d) — More Appropriate for a 20-Year Participating Endowment

Co-insurance is typically more appropriate for a 20-year participating endowment.

Reason: A participating endowment accumulates a substantial policy reserve over its 20-year term. By year 15, the reserve might be 70–80% of the sum assured — leaving a NAR of only 20–30%. Under YRT, the reinsurer's coverage declines significantly over time as the NAR reduces — providing less protection precisely when the mortality risk of an older life is highest. Under co-insurance, the reinsurer shares the entire policy (including the reserve) — providing proportional mortality protection regardless of reserve levels, which is more appropriate for a long-duration savings-and-protection product.

Additionally, co-insurance's upfront ceding commission helps the cedant manage new business strain on participating endowments, which have high first-year acquisition costs.
Part (e) — IFRS 17 Accounting Treatment Differences

Under IFRS 17:

Co-insurance: The ceded co-insurance treaty is a reinsurance contract held by the cedant. Under IFRS 17, it is measured as a group of reinsurance contracts — the cedant recognises a reinsurance asset (the present value of future recoveries from the reinsurer, risk-adjusted). A reinsurance CSM is recognised if the treaty is in the cedant's favour. Changes in the cedant's underlying policy liabilities (if from new information) are reflected in the reinsurance asset.

YRT: Also measured as a reinsurance contract held. However, the YRT's measurement is simpler because it has no reserve cession — the reinsurance asset reflects only the present value of expected future mortality recoveries. The Year-of-Coverage approach under IFRS 17 (for short-duration reinsurance that renews annually) may apply, simplifying the measurement.

questions.stem:
A life insurer’s YRT treaty with its reinsurer is approaching renewal. The reinsurer has indicated it will increase the rate factor (the multiple of the treaty mortality table) from 85% to 110% for the coming year, citing adverse mortality experience on the cedant’s group life portfolio over the past three years.
(a) Explain the financial impact of this rate increase on the insurer’s claims costs and profitability.
(b) Describe the negotiating options available to the cedant.
(c) Explain why the domestic cession obligations under NIIRA 2025 both constrain and assist the cedant in this negotiation.
(d) If the cedant cannot negotiate an acceptable rate, describe the capital and risk management implications of reducing reinsurance coverage or increasing its retention limit instead.

model.h: Part (a) — Financial Impact of the Rate Increase

The rate factor is the multiple applied to the treaty's standard mortality table to calculate the annual YRT risk premium. An increase from 85% to 110% represents a 29.4% increase in the YRT risk premium cost.

Financial impact example: If the current YRT risk premium is ₦500m per annum (at 85% of table), the new premium at 110% is:
₦500m × (110/85) = ₦500m × 1.294 = ₦647m per annum

Additional annual cost: ₦147m — a direct hit to the insurer's underwriting profit. If the insurer's current net profit on the reinsured portfolio is ₦300m, the additional reinsurance cost reduces profit by nearly 50%.

The increase also signals that the reinsurer believes the cedant's mortality experience is materially adverse — a concern the insurer must investigate independently.
Part (b) — Negotiating Options for the Cedant

1. Dispute the experience data: Request the reinsurer's detailed mortality experience data for the portfolio. If the cedant believes the reinsurer's characterisation of the experience is inaccurate (e.g., including claims from outside the treaty scope), the data can be challenged.

2. Partial rate concession: Negotiate a smaller increase (e.g., to 95%) in exchange for a commitment to address the underlying mortality experience — enhanced underwriting controls, FCL reductions, or portfolio restructuring.

3. Tranche renewal: Accept the increased rate for part of the portfolio (high-mortality segments) while seeking better terms for lower-risk segments (smaller sums assured, younger lives).

4. Alternative reinsurer: Obtain competing treaty quotes from other YRT providers. The ability to threaten replacement is the cedant's strongest negotiating lever, particularly if the portfolio has sound fundamentals despite a difficult claims year.

5. Treaty restructuring: Convert from YRT to co-insurance for part of the portfolio — potentially at a less adverse pricing point if the reinsurer's co-insurance appetite is stronger than its YRT appetite.
Part (c) — NIIRA 2025 Domestic Cession Obligation

NIIRA 2025 requires Nigerian life insurers to offer a defined percentage of their reinsurance cession to domestic reinsurers (primarily NRC — Nigeria Re) before approaching international reinsurers. This provision:

Constrains the cedant: The domestic cession obligation limits the cedant's freedom to place 100% of the treaty with the best-priced international reinsurer. If domestic reinsurers (at the ₦35 bn capital level) charge above-market rates, the cedant cannot entirely avoid this cost.

Assists the cedant: The domestic cession requirement gives the cedant a leverage point with the international reinsurer. If the international reinsurer's rate increase is excessive, the cedant can credibly threaten to redirect more cession to the domestic market — reducing the international reinsurer's premium volume and therefore its appetite to demand aggressively elevated rates. Additionally, if the domestic reinsurer offers YRT at below the international rate increase, the cedant can substitute part of the international capacity with domestic capacity, limiting the overall premium impact.
Part (d) — Capital and Risk Management Implications of Reducing Reinsurance or Increasing Retention

If the cedant decides to reduce reinsurance coverage (accept the rate but reduce the ceded volume) or increase its retention limit (retain more risk per life):

1. Capital requirement increases: Under NIIRA 2025's RBC framework, C2 (insurance risk) capital is based on the net retained mortality exposure. Reducing reinsurance increases net exposure, which mechanically increases the C2 RBC charge, which increases the total capital required. If the insurer is already running close to its RBC minimum, this may not be feasible.

2. Solvency ratio impact: The increased C2 capital requirement reduces the solvency ratio — the ratio of available capital to required capital. A ratio that falls below NAICOM's minimum triggers regulatory intervention.

3. Concentration risk: Retaining a larger net amount per individual life increases concentration risk — a cluster of large deaths could produce claims far above the expected annual average, creating volatility in results.

4. Board approval required: A decision to materially increase the net retention limit is a risk appetite decision requiring Board Risk Committee review and Board approval, with the Statutory Actuary's assessment of the capital and solvency implications.
Thesis

The ₦35 billion reinsurer minimum capital requirement is the most ambitious single capital threshold in NIIRA 2025 — an increase of more than threefold on the previous ₦10bn. It reflects a deliberate policy choice to transform the domestic reinsurance sector from a market of numerous small, lightly capitalised domestic cession recipients into a concentrated, genuinely capable risk retention market. The transformation is correct in principle; its costs and risks must be managed through a combination of NAICOM oversight and the industry's willingness to consolidate rather than comply on paper.
(a) Rationale and Market Development Objectives

1. Genuine capacity vs nominal capacity: Multiple domestic reinsurers operating with ₦10bn capital could each only support modest retained exposures. A domestic reinsurer with ₦35 bn capital can underwrite significantly larger risks, provide more meaningful treaty capacity, and absorb major loss events without financial distress.

2. Premium retention: NAICOM's objective is to retain more Nigerian insurance premium income within Nigeria's financial system rather than exporting it to international reinsurers as foreign exchange outflows. A credibly capitalised domestic market can absorb more risk domestically.

3. Technical capacity building: Larger, better-capitalised reinsurers can invest in actuarial expertise, risk modelling capability, and data infrastructure that smaller operators cannot afford. This builds genuine domestic reinsurance technical capacity over time.

4. Financial stability: Inadequately capitalised domestic reinsurers are susceptible to insolvency under catastrophic loss scenarios, creating systemic risk within the cedant market. Higher capital requirements reduce this systemic vulnerability.
(b) Consolidation Dynamics

The ₦35 bn threshold will force consolidation among domestic reinsurers. Nigeria's domestic reinsurance market at NIIRA 2025's commencement comprised a small number of licensed domestic reinsurers, most with capital well below ₦35 bn.

Expected consolidation outcomes:
1. Mergers between domestic reinsurers: Two or three smaller domestic reinsurers merging to achieve the ₦35 bn threshold jointly creates a combined entity with greater capacity and technical depth.
2. Capital injection by strategic investors: International reinsurers (African Re, Munich Re, Swiss Re) may see the NIIRA 2025 recapitalisation as an opportunity to acquire or partner with domestic reinsurers and establish a stronger Nigerian market presence.
3. Exit by non-compliant operators: Reinsurers unable to raise ₦35 bn within the compliance period must surrender their licences — reducing market participants.

The Nigerian direct insurer market post-2007 recapitalisation went from 103 to 49 companies — a similar consolidation dynamic is likely in reinsurance.
(c) Implications for Life Insurers

Fewer but better-capitalised domestic reinsurers create both opportunities and challenges for cedant life insurers:

Opportunities:
1. Higher treaty capacity: A ₦35 bn domestic reinsurer can provide larger per-risk and aggregate treaty capacities — reducing the frequency with which cedants must turn to expensive facultative international reinsurance for large risks.
2. Technical support: Well-capitalised domestic reinsurers can invest in underwriting manuals, mortality table development, claims investigation support, and product pricing guidance — services that their international counterparts provide but that smaller domestic operators cannot.
3. AML/regulatory alignment: Domestic reinsurers operating under NAICOM supervision provide cedants with a domestic cession counterparty that is subject to the same regulatory framework — reducing the compliance complexity of international cession.

Challenges:
1. Pricing discipline: Fewer domestic reinsurers means reduced price competition. If two or three dominant domestic reinsurers set YRT rates above international market rates, cedants' treaty costs increase.
2. Counterparty concentration: With fewer domestic reinsurers, cedants' counterparty concentration risk increases — the failure of one major domestic reinsurer would have systemic consequences.
(d) Tension Between Domestic Cession and International Capacity

The domestic cession obligation creates a structural tension for cedants writing very large individual life risks:

1. Capacity limitation: Even a ₦35 bn domestic reinsurer can only provide limited per-risk capacity for a ₦1bn individual life policy. International reinsurers with global balance sheets can absorb this risk — domestic reinsurers cannot.

2. Technical expertise: For specialist risks (offshore oil workers, aviation professionals, high-risk occupations), international reinsurers maintain the most current mortality data and underwriting guidelines. Domestic reinsurers' technical capacity for these risks is limited.

3. Compliance cost: The domestic cession obligation requires cedants to offer a portion of every qualifying reinsurance cession to domestic reinsurers before approaching international markets — creating administrative burden and potentially slowing the placement of time-sensitive large risks.

Resolution pathway: NAICOM should clarify the interaction between the domestic cession obligation and the technical capacity limitation for very large risks. A clear framework — allowing immediate international placement for risks above a defined threshold (e.g., ₦500m per life net of domestic treaty) — would preserve the domestic cession objective for the majority of risks while acknowledging the genuine capacity constraints at the top of the market.

questions.stem: ‘For a Nigerian life insurer, reinsurance is not merely a risk management tool — it is a strategic enabler of growth, a source of actuarial expertise, and a capital management lever that directly affects the company’s ability to compete in the market.’ Critically evaluate this proposition. In your answer, discuss: the role of reinsurance in expanding the insurer’s capacity to write large individual life and group life risks; the value of reinsurer technical support in a market where domestic actuarial and underwriting expertise is scarce; the capital management function of reinsurance under the NIIRA 2025 RBC framework; and the governance and operational standards required to ensure that the reinsurance programme delivers its intended strategic benefits and does not become a source of financial or regulatory risk.

model.h: Thesis

The proposition is correct and understates the case: for a Nigerian life insurer operating with limited capital, a shallow domestic actuarial talent pool, and an underdeveloped product development infrastructure, a well-structured reinsurance programme is not a peripheral risk management tool — it is a foundational strategic asset that determines the insurer's ability to compete, price accurately, and grow sustainably.
Capacity Expansion

Without reinsurance, a Nigerian life insurer with ₦10bn capital and a ₦3.5bn net solvency margin can prudently offer perhaps ₦500m maximum per individual life — limiting its ability to compete for keyman covers, group schemes for large employers, or high-net-worth individual policies.

With a well-structured treaty programme (surplus treaty + YRT + per-life XL), the same insurer can write individual policies up to ₦2–5bn, group schemes with total sum assureds of ₦500bn+, and credit life portfolios for large lending institutions — accessing premium volumes that are 5–10× what the raw capital base would permit. This capacity multiplier is the most direct mechanism through which reinsurance enables growth.

In the Nigerian context, market share in group life (where the largest schemes are state government or major corporate schemes) is won by the insurer that can provide the largest FCL and the deepest reinsurance capacity. Reinsurance access is therefore directly correlated with competitive positioning in the most valuable segments of the market.
Actuarial and Underwriting Technical Support

Nigeria's life insurance industry faces a chronic actuarial and underwriting talent shortage. The large international reinsurers — Munich Re, Swiss Re, Hannover Re, Africa Re — provide extensive technical support to their cedant relationships as part of the treaty partnership:

1. Mortality data: International reinsurers maintain pan-African insured life mortality databases that are more current and more granular than the EFU tables. They provide cedants with guidance on appropriate mortality loadings for specific target markets, occupations, and health conditions.

2. Underwriting manuals: Reinsurers develop and update detailed underwriting guidelines (medical, financial, occupational) that small insurers would not have the resources to maintain internally. Cedants adopting reinsurer underwriting guidelines benefit from globally benchmarked standards.

3. Product development: Major reinsurers have product development teams that help cedants design new life products — particularly for the digital/Insurtech distribution space — providing actuarial pricing support, lapse rate benchmarks, and benefit design guidance.

4. Claims support: For complex or large claims, reinsurers provide claims investigation support and second opinions — particularly valuable for critical illness claims with contested medical definitions.

This technical support is a material subsidy to the cedant's internal capability. For a smaller Nigerian life insurer without a full actuarial function, the reinsurer relationship may be the primary source of actuarial and technical knowledge.
Capital Management Under NIIRA 2025 RBC

Under NIIRA 2025's RBC framework, reinsurance is an explicit capital management lever:

1. C2 (Insurance Risk) reduction: Reinsurance reduces the net mortality exposure, directly reducing the C2 component of the RBC requirement. For every ₦1bn of net sum assured ceded, the C2 capital requirement falls — freeing capital for other uses (writing more business, improving the solvency ratio).

2. Capital efficiency: An insurer that is constrained by its RBC minimum can write more business by increasing reinsurance — effectively buying capital through the treaty relationship. This is 'off-balance-sheet capital' in the practical sense.

3. Solvency ratio management: An insurer approaching the NAICOM minimum solvency ratio can use a reinsurance treaty restructuring (increasing quota share or YRT cession percentages) to reduce the net exposure and restore the solvency ratio above the regulatory floor — buying time for capital raising or business restructuring.

Risk: Over-reliance on reinsurance for capital management creates counterparty concentration risk. If the key reinsurer withdraws or becomes insolvent, the cedant's net exposure surges — potentially breaching the RBC minimum. NAICOM's Reinsurance Guidelines require cedants to monitor reinsurer counterparty ratings and diversify their reinsurance panel.
Governance and Operational Standards

For reinsurance to deliver its strategic benefits, the insurer must maintain governance standards that ensure the programme is properly structured, monitored, and complied with:

1. Board approval: The Board should approve the overall reinsurance strategy (retention limits, treaty structure, counterparty criteria) as part of the risk appetite framework. Annual Board review of the reinsurance programme's adequacy is minimum governance practice.

2. Reinsurance treaty compliance: The cedant must comply with all treaty warranties (bordereaux submission timescales, claim reporting requirements, premium settlement). Treaty breach can invalidate the reinsurance coverage — leaving the cedant exposed to uncovered losses.

3. Counterparty management: The insurer must monitor the credit rating of all reinsurance counterparties. A reinsurer that deteriorates from A-rated to B-rated creates a counterparty risk exposure that must be disclosed in the ORSA and potentially hedged by diversifying to stronger counterparties.

4. Claims recovery management: Active pursuit of reinsurance recoveries is an operational discipline — slow recovery of reinsured claims impacts cash flow and may generate disputed amounts if treaty reporting requirements are not met. A dedicated reinsurance accounting function is a governance requirement for any insurer with material treaty exposure.
